## Who Were the Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?

### Research Question and Conclusion

This argument addresses the parentage of Patrick Flynn, who was born about 1845, most likely in Ireland based on census evidence, and who died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Three independent original sources, examined together, establish at the **probable** level that his father was **Thomas Flynn** of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Evidence for his mother's identity is insufficient to conclude — the candidate, Bridget Flynn, is documented only by a speculative identity inference with a near-zero evidentiary basis, and no record in the project names her as either Patrick's mother or Thomas's wife. The paternity conclusion is recorded at probable rather than proved because research has not been declared exhaustive and several record types remain unsearched.

---

### I. Paternity: Thomas Flynn

#### A. Death Certificate — Direct Secondary Evidence

Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (certificate no. 4521) names **Thomas Flynn** as his father.[^1] This is original-source, direct evidence of the relationship. The informant, however, was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law — a family member not present at Patrick's birth and reporting parentage facts secondhand, likely from family tradition. The information is therefore classified as **secondary**: it originates from someone without personal knowledge of the birth event. Secondary parentage information on death certificates is a well-known genealogical limitation, but it is not discarded for that reason; it carries the weight of family knowledge and is corroborated here by independent census evidence from Patrick's own lifetime.

[^1]: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

#### B. 1860 Census — Independent Corroborating Indirect Evidence

The 1860 U.S. Census for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 112, family 119, lists Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, as a member of the household headed by **Thomas Flynn**.[^2] The 1860 census did not include a relationship column (that column was not introduced until the 1880 census), so the parent-child relationship is **inferred** from household position, shared surname, age consistency (a 15-year-old in 1860 would have been born about 1845, matching Patrick's known birth year), and birthplace consistency. This is indirect evidence of the relationship, extracted from an original, contemporary source. Patrick's presence in this household a decade after the 1850 enumeration below rules out chance co-enumeration as an explanation.

[^2]: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

#### C. 1850 Census — Independent Corroborating Indirect Evidence

The 1850 U.S. Census for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 84, family 91, lists a child of approximately age 5 (consistent with birth ~1845) in the household of **Thomas Flynn**.[^3] The 1850 census does not state relationships and does not name the child in the set of assertions linked to the parentage question — the name assertion (a_001) was extracted for a separate question and carries its own person-evidence link (pe_001). What the 1850 census contributes here is the co-enumeration at age 5 in a Thomas Flynn household in Schuylkill County — indirect evidence corroborating the 1860 household placement ten years later.

[^3]: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.

#### D. Correlation and Source Analysis

The three sources are independent of one another: two are population censuses created by federal enumerators in 1850 and 1860; the third is a vital record created by a state health department in 1908 based on an informant report. None derives from another. They agree: all three are consistent with Thomas Flynn being the father of a Patrick Flynn born about 1845, living in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

The death certificate provides the only **direct** statement of the relationship. Taken alone, secondary direct evidence from a son-in-law informant would not be sufficient to conclude at probable. But it is corroborated by two independent censuses showing the same Patrick Flynn residing in Thomas Flynn's household during childhood and adolescence — exactly when a father-son relationship would predict co-residence. The convergence of independent sources — two original federal population schedules and an original state vital record — across a 58-year span, pointing consistently to the same man as father, supports a probable conclusion.

#### E. Shortfall

The paternity conclusion does not reach **proved** because research has not been declared exhaustive. Schuylkill County probate records for Thomas Flynn have not yet been searched; a Thomas Flynn estate file naming Patrick as an heir would independently confirm the relationship. The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses have not been searched for Patrick as an adult. Church and parish registers for the Schuylkill County area, which may record baptism, marriage, or burial entries linking Patrick to Thomas, have not been searched. These records, if found, would most likely corroborate the conclusion. The absence of a probate search is the most consequential gap — probate records can both confirm paternity and identify the mother — but the current evidence already preponderates toward Thomas without it.

---

### II. Maternity: Bridget Flynn — Not Proved

The project identified a candidate mother: **Bridget Flynn**, a widow, age 52, enumerated in Schuylkill County in the 1870 census.[^4] Her hypothesis (h_002) was assigned a match score of 0.0002 — effectively speculative — by the person-evidence assessor. This section explains why maternity cannot be concluded.

[^4]: 1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

The entire basis for treating this Bridget Flynn as Patrick's mother rests on two facts: (1) her surname is Flynn, and (2) she is enumerated as a widow in the same county where Thomas Flynn was known to have lived. Neither fact connects her to Thomas (I2) or to Patrick (I1). "Flynn" is a common Irish surname in Schuylkill County, and widowhood in 1870 of a woman age ~52 is consistent with having been married during the 1840s — but so would be any same-surname widow of approximately the right age in the county. She does not appear in Thomas Flynn's 1850 or 1860 household in the evidence gathered. No children are listed in her 1870 household. No death or marriage record for Thomas Flynn's wife has been located.

Until at least one of these is found, maternity remains unresolved.

---

### III. Conclusion
